faqs.question: What is the difference between a shayari and a quote?
faqs.answer: A sher is a metrical unit: two lines of matched length, a rhyme word (qafiya) and usually a repeated tail phrase (radif). A quote has no such obligations. That is why a quote translated into two lines with a line break in the middle still does not sound like shayari.

faqs.question: How do I propose a girl in shayari without sounding fake?
faqs.answer: Pick a line whose vocabulary matches how the two of you already talk, and say something in your own words either side of it. A sher lands as sincere when it condenses a feeling you have already shown, and as performance when it is the first sincere thing you have said.

faqs.question: Should I send the shayari in Devanagari or in Roman English?
faqs.answer: Send both, in that order, if she reads Devanagari at all. Most of this audience types in Roman and reads in Devanagari, so the Devanagari carries the weight and the Roman guarantees she can sound it out.

faqs.question: Is it okay to send a shayari written by a famous poet?
faqs.answer: It is normal practice, and reciting someone else's sher is part of the culture — but attribute it. Sending a Faiz or a Ghalib couplet unattributed and letting her assume you wrote it is the one version that backfires badly if she recognises it.

faqs.question: What does radif mean in shayari?
faqs.answer: Radif is the phrase that repeats unchanged at the end of both lines, after the rhyme word. In 'ghar lagta hai' and 'safar lagta hai', the radif is 'lagta hai'. Not every sher has one; when it does, it is the part your ear recognises as a pattern.

faqs.question: What is qafiya in simple words?
faqs.answer: Qafiya is the rhyme word itself — 'ghar' and 'safar' in the pair above. A 2020 paper in the Indian Journal of Science and Technology calls it the element without which a piece is not Hindi/Urdu poetry at all. If both your lines end on the same word, you have repetition, not qafiya.

faqs.question: How long should a propose shayari be?
faqs.answer: Two lines. One sher is a complete unit and is meant to be readable alone, so stacking four or six of them dilutes it. If you want more length, put your own prose around one sher rather than adding a second one.

faqs.question: What if my girlfriend does not read Hindi or Urdu?
faqs.answer: Then shayari is the wrong form and no amount of transliteration fixes it. Send the English sense on its own, or write something plain — a sher she has to decode is a puzzle at the exact moment she should be feeling something.

faqs.question: Should I say the shayari out loud or send it as a message?
faqs.answer: Out loud if you can, because the form was built for recitation — a mushaira is an audience listening, not reading. A message is the honest fallback for long distance, and it has one advantage: she can reread it.

faqs.question: Can I use these lines for Propose Day?
faqs.answer: Yes. Propose Day 2027 falls on Monday 8 February, the second day of Valentine week, which lands mid-working-day for most people — so plan for a message or a call rather than an evening, unless you are meeting anyway.

faqs.question: What do I do if she does not reply to the shayari?
faqs.answer: Do not send a second one. A sher is an opening, and a silence after it usually means she is deciding, not that she missed it — following up with more verse converts a question into pressure.

faqs.question: Do I have to write my own shayari, or can I use these?
faqs.answer: These eight are original and written for this page, so you can use them as they stand. If you do change a word, check that the rhyme word and the syllable count both survive — most edits break one or the other.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Propose Girlfriend Shayari, and How a Sher Actually Works

A propose girlfriend shayari is a **sher** — a self-contained two-line unit with a rhyme word (*qafiya*) and usually a repeated tail phrase (*radif*) — not a caption with line breaks in it. That distinction is why most copy-pasted lines land flat. SubhSandesh has recorded 4,567 personalised pages built since 12 March 2026 across 16 page types, and platform-wide the most-created is the "I love you" page at 1,138 builds, 24.9% of the total. Below: what makes a sher work, eight original lines in Devanagari with Roman and English, and which register suits whom.

## What a sher actually is

A sher is one couplet. Both lines share a metre; the second lands the turn. In a ghazal the shers are strung by rhyme, not plot — a 2011 University of Texas study notes that its couplets are [thematically unrelated yet metrically and prosodically related](https://archive.org/download/ghazal-canonizationand-translation/Ambiguity%20and%20Semantics%20in%20the%20Urdu%20ghazal.pdf), so any single sher can be lifted out and stand alone.

So sending one couplet is not an excerpt; it is the unit working as designed. But note what the form inherited. The [ghazal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghazal) came into Urdu from a Persian model, and Agnieszka Kuczkiewicz-Fraś, in *Urdu Studies* in 2020, describes its ishq as [experienced in separation and never fulfilled](https://urdustudies.in/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/Urdu-Studies-2020-Fras.pdf), pain its distinctive mark. Classical shayari is built to ache. You are trying to get a yes.

## How to tell a good sher from a bad one

Four things, and you can hear all four.

**Qafiya** is the rhyme word. A 2020 paper in the *Indian Journal of Science and Technology*, built on a 13.46-million-token Hindi–Urdu poetry corpus, calls qafiya [the core element without which a piece is not Hindi/Urdu poetry at all](https://indjst.org/articles/edit-distance-based-search-approach-for-retrieving-element-wise-prosodyrhymes-in-hindi-urdu-poetry) — merely writing. The same paper defines **radif** as the phrasal suffix following the qafiya, repeated unchanged.

So in *ghar lagta hai* / *safar lagta hai*, the qafiya is *ghar*/*safar* and the radif *lagta hai*. If your two rhyme words are the same word, you have no qafiya — the commonest failure in a copy-pasted line.

**Matla** is the opening couplet, where both lines rhyme. Every line below is a matla: a sher sent alone needs both lines to chime, or the rhyme lands against nothing.

**Bahr** is metre. Classical scansion counts long and short syllables; the lines below are matched by syllable count instead — an approximation, not the same thing. Read each pair aloud: if one line outruns the other, the sher limps.

## 8 propose shayari lines for a girlfriend, with the register marked

Eight originals, written for this page: Devanagari, Roman, English sense, and who each suits.

### 1. The one that admits the delay

बहुत दिन चुप रहा, मगर अब कह रहा हूँ,
तेरे बिन हर एक दिन अधूरा रह रहा हूँ।

*bahut din chup raha, magar ab keh raha hoon,*
*tere bin har ek din adhoora reh raha hoon.*

"I stayed quiet a long time; I am saying it now — without you every day of mine stays unfinished."

Register: plain Hindi. Qafiya *keh*/*reh*, radif *raha hoon*. Suits a first confession to someone who reads no Urdu register.

### 2. The Urdu-lite one

तेरे बग़ैर ये दिल भी वीरान लगता है,
तेरा ख़याल ही मेरी पहचान लगता है।

*tere baghair ye dil bhi veeran lagta hai,*
*tera khayal hi meri pehchaan lagta hai.*

"Without you this heart feels deserted; the thought of you feels like my identity."

Register: *baghair*, *veeran*, *khayal* are Perso-Arabic, carried into everyday Hindi by film songs. Qafiya *veeran*/*pehchaan*, radif *lagta hai*. Safe for anyone.

### 3. The one that does not pressure her

सवाल तो मेरा है, जवाब तुम्हारा है,
जल्दी कोई नहीं — ये वक़्त हमारा है।

*sawaal to mera hai, jawaab tumhara hai,*
*jaldi koi nahin — ye waqt hamara hai.*

"The question is mine, the answer yours. No hurry — this time belongs to us both."

Register: neutral; *sawaal*, *jawaab*, *waqt* are universal. Qafiya *tumhara*/*hamara*, radif *hai*. Suits a real proposal she should feel free to refuse.

### 4. The one instead of a gift

न फूल है, न मोती, न कोई नज़राना है,
बस एक सच्ची बात है, बस एक ठिकाना है।

*na phool hai, na moti, na koi nazrana hai,*
*bas ek sachchi baat hai, bas ek thikana hai.*

"No flower, no pearl, no offering — one true thing to say, and one place to belong."

Register: *nazrana* is a mild step up in formality; the rest is plain. Qafiya *nazrana*/*thikana*, radif *hai*. For an empty-handed ask.

### 5. The one for a girlfriend of years

ये साथ बरसों का भी नया लगता है,
तेरा हर लफ़्ज़ मुझको दुआ लगता है।

*ye saath barson ka bhi naya lagta hai,*
*tera har lafz mujhko dua lagta hai.*

"Years together still feel new; every word of yours feels like a blessing."

Register: *lafz*, *dua* are Urdu-origin, widely understood. Qafiya *naya*/*dua*, radif *lagta hai*. Suits a long relationship, not a first ask.

### 6. The one about being afraid

डर है कि कहीं बात बदल न जाए,
पर चुप रहा तो उम्र निकल न जाए।

*dar hai ki kahin baat badal na jaaye,*
*par chup raha to umr nikal na jaaye.*

"I fear what we have might change; but if I stay quiet, a life slips past."

Register: plain Hindi. Qafiya *badal*/*nikal*, radif *na jaaye*. Suits proposing to a friend, where risk is the subject.

### 7. The one for distance

तू मिले तो हर रास्ता घर लगता है,
तू न हो तो घर भी सफ़र लगता है।

*tu mile to har raasta ghar lagta hai,*
*tu na ho to ghar bhi safar lagta hai.*

"When you are here every road feels like home; when you are not, home feels like a journey."

Register: neutral, one Perso-Arabic word (*safar*). Qafiya *ghar*/*safar*, radif *lagta hai*. Suits long distance, or a proposal before a move.

### 8. The properly Urdu one

तेरी क़ुर्बत का कोई भी मोल नहीं है,
मेरे पास तेरे बिन कोई बोल नहीं है।

*teri qurbat ka koi bhi mol nahin hai,*
*mere paas tere bin koi bol nahin hai.*

"No worth can be set on your nearness; without you I have no words."

Register: *qurbat* is genuine Urdu register; many Hindi readers will not know it. Qafiya *mol*/*bol*, radif *nahin hai*. Send only to someone who reads that vocabulary.

Five more were drafted and cut: one turned on *kaho na*, which reads as both "say no" and "do say"; one broke gender agreement between *inaam* and *teri*; one repeated its rhyme word; one wobbled its tense; one had no qafiya once pulled from its ghazal.

## Which register suits whom

Register is the decision most shayari pages never mention. These eight fall into four bands.

| Register band | Lines here | Vocabulary example | Risk if mismatched |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plain Hindi | 1, 6 | *chup*, *adhoora*, *badal* | None; may read plain |
| Urdu-lite (film-song) | 2, 5, 7 | *khayal*, *lafz*, *safar* | Very low in North India |
| Urdu register | 8 | *qurbat*, *unwaan* | Reads as showing off if those words are not hers |
| Neutral / no-pressure | 3, 4 | *sawaal*, *jawaab*, *thikana* | None; least poetic band |

Bands one, two and four are safe by default. Band three is a choice about her, not about you.

That mismatch has a history. Hiba Mirza, in a 2014 *International Journal of Humanities and Social Science* study of Delhi mushairas, records that older practice used [obsolete and difficult words to highlight the vocabulary skills of the poet](https://ijhss.thebrpi.org/journals/Vol_4_No_10_August_2014/22.pdf), and that this excluded the masses — while today's mushairas prefer simpler language. Your proposal is a mushaira with one listener.

A rhymed line also feels more *true* than the same sentence unrhymed. McGlone and Tofighbakhsh, in *Poetics* in 1999, had people rate unfamiliar aphorisms in rhyming and non-rhyming forms of identical meaning; both were judged equally comprehensible, but the [rhyming versions were perceived as more accurate](https://gwern.net/doc/psychology/cognitive-bias/1999-mcglone.pdf). That is shayari's quiet mechanism, and a warning: rhyme buys credibility your sentence has not earned.

## तू, तुम or आप — the pronoun carries more than the vocabulary

Lines 1, 2, 5, 7 and 8 use *tu*/*tera*; lines 3 and 4 use *tum*/*tumhara*. Not an accident.

*Tu* is the intimate second person: right for a girlfriend of years, presumptuous towards someone you have not asked yet. *Tum* is warm and safe. *Aap* is respectful and usually too formal for a proposal.

Swapping a pronoun breaks the metre, so do not just substitute the word. Line 7 in *tum* becomes *tum milo to har raasta ghar lagta hai* — a syllable longer, and it limps. Rewrite or pick another.

## Where a page beats a message, and where it does not

If the sher is the whole gesture, send the sher. One couplet in a chat at the right moment is often exactly correct, and no page improves on it.

A page earns its place when the sher opens something longer. If you are asking her to marry you, the [proposal scrapbook page that ends in a YES button](/proposal) gives the couplet somewhere to sit: your story first, the question last. If this is "will you be my girlfriend", the [romantic "I love you" page](/love-gf) is the honest fit.

What SubhSandesh can and cannot tell you about those routes:

| Route for the sher | First-party usage | Median first-save to last-edit | Password-protected before sharing |
|---|---|---|---|
| "I love you" page | 1,138 pages, 24.9% of 4,567, platform-wide | 6.4 hours, n = 1,138, sampled on /love-gf | 39.9%, platform-wide (1,822 of 4,567) |
| Proposal scrapbook page | no proposal-specific figure exists | not measured | 39.9%, platform-wide (1,822 of 4,567) |
| One sher in a chat | not measured | n/a | n/a |

Every figure above is platform-wide across 16 page types, or sampled on /love-gf. No proposal-page data exists, so none is quoted.

The case against a page at all: if she does not read Devanagari comfortably, a page full of it is a wall, not a gift. If the relationship is in trouble, a sher is decoration on an unresolved problem. To see what else exists, [browse the full template list](/templates) — but a well-chosen couplet, sent alone, is not the lesser choice.

## Sources

- Kirk, *Half-Drawn Arrows of Meaning*, UT Austin, 2011.
- Kuczkiewicz-Fraś, "Urdu Ghazal: The Poetic String of Pearls", *Urdu Studies*, 2020.
- Khan and others, "Edit distance-based search approach for element-wise prosody/rhymes in Hindi-Urdu poetry", *Indian Journal of Science and Technology*, 9 November 2020.
- Mirza, "The Role of Poetry Readings in Dispelling the Notion that Urdu is a Muslim Language", *IJHSS*, August 2014.
- McGlone and Tofighbakhsh, "The Keats heuristic: Rhyme as reason in aphorism interpretation", *Poetics* 26, 1999.

auditReport.honestAssessment: Every incumbent on this SERP is an undifferentiated dump of lines — the five pages checked run 500 to 5,100 words, none defines qafiya, radif or matla, none gives a Roman transliteration next to the Devanagari, and none tells the reader which register suits which recipient. This page is the only one that does all four, and the only one that names the five lines it cut and why. That is a real citation hook for an answer engine asked 'what is radif in shayari' or 'is this sher correct'. It will not beat MensXP, Zee or the shayari farms on the head term: they refresh every February and their domain authority is far above ours, so position 6–10 on 'propose girlfriend shayari' is the realistic target, with the form-explainer sub-queries the likelier win. The lines are matched by syllable count, not classical arūz scansion, which is stated in the body and is a genuine limitation.
